body:
Why Gandhi prescribed the eleven vows

Gandhi treated ethical discipline as necessary for a life devoted to truth, non-violence and service. His ashram communities used a set of 11 vows, also called observances, to guide the conduct of their members.

These vows were intended to shape everyday behaviour. They concerned honesty, restraint, possessions, work, courage and relations with other people. They should be understood as ethical commitments, not as a list of 11 laws enacted by a government.

A significant Gujarat connection is the Satyagraha Ashram at Kochrab, Ahmedabad, founded by Gandhi in 1915. The ashram was later shifted to Sabarmati. The observances were associated with the discipline of life and service practised in these ashram communities.

The first 6 vows

The following vows are presented in the order used in the Rajghat Samadhi Committee's account of the ashram observances.

VowMeaningEveryday identification
SatyaTruthfulness in thought, speech and actionCorrecting an inaccurate statement even when the correction is personally inconvenient
AhimsaNon-violence and active goodwill towards othersOpposing an unfair decision without threats, cruelty or revenge
BrahmacharyaChastity and disciplined control of sexual desires and the sensesMaintaining the personal restraint required by an ethical commitment
AsvadaControl of the palate; restraint in eating for pleasure aloneEating according to bodily need rather than continually seeking indulgence in taste
AsteyaNon-stealing; not taking or misusing what one is not entitled to useReturning a borrowed book on time and using it only as permitted
AparigrahaNon-possession; avoiding unnecessary accumulationRefraining from hoarding goods beyond reasonable needs

Understanding the important distinctions

Satya and ahimsa

Satya asks whether conduct is truthful. Ahimsa asks whether it avoids injury and expresses goodwill. An honest statement is not automatically non-violent if it is delivered with the deliberate intention of humiliating someone.

Brahmacharya and asvada

Brahmacharya concerns chastity and self-restraint. In the ashram setting it carried a demanding discipline regarding sexual conduct and the control of desires. Asvada is a more specific observance concerning the sense of taste and the purpose of eating.

Both involve restraint, but asvada should not be mistaken for the whole meaning of brahmacharya. A statement specifically about avoiding indulgence in food points most directly to asvada.

Asteya and aparigraha

These 2 vows are particularly easy to confuse because both restrict excessive claims over material things.

Asteya means non-stealing. Gandhi applied it more widely than the prohibition against secretly taking someone's property. Misusing something entrusted for a particular purpose or retaining a borrowed object longer than permitted also conflicts with this observance.

Aparigraha means non-possession. It asks a person to avoid accumulating or retaining more than is reasonably needed. An object may have been acquired lawfully, yet keeping it unnecessarily can still conflict with the ideal of non-possession.

Consider a borrowed book. Returning it within the agreed period illustrates asteya. Consider several unnecessary objects already owned by a person. Choosing not to hoard them illustrates aparigraha. The first example concerns respecting another person's entitlement; the second concerns limiting one's own unnecessary possessions.

The relationship between self-discipline and service

These observances are not unrelated rules. Truthfulness governs honesty; non-violence governs the treatment of others; brahmacharya and asvada govern desires; and asteya and aparigraha govern the acquisition and use of material things.

Together, they express Gandhi's view that public service should rest on disciplined personal conduct. A person who speaks about welfare while knowingly deceiving others or misusing entrusted resources has not satisfied these ethical requirements.

Prelims focus

  • The ashram observances comprised 11 vows.
  • The Satyagraha Ashram was established at Kochrab, Ahmedabad, in 1915 and later shifted to Sabarmati.
  • Brahmacharya: chastity and discipline of the senses.
  • Asvada: control of the palate.
  • Asteya: non-stealing; Aparigraha: non-possession.
  • Trap: Lawful ownership of an unnecessary object does not automatically satisfy the ideal of aparigraha.

[Sources: Rajghat Samadhi Committee, Government of India, The Eleven Vows of Gandhi Ji, introductory account of the Kochrab Ashram and observances I–VI, consulted 22 November 2026; Mani Bhavan Gandhi Sangrahalaya, Gandhi's Eleven Vows, explanations of Satya, Ahimsa, Brahmacharya, Asvada, Asteya and Aparigraha, consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Gandhi's Eleven Ashram Vows: Truth, Self-discipline and Simplicity

body:
The remaining 5 vows

Gandhi's 11 ashram observances included commitments relating not only to individual restraint but also to work, the immediate community and respectful relations among people. The remaining 5 vows complete the set.

VowMeaningEveryday identification
Sharir-shrama or Bread LabourUseful physical labour as a personal responsibilityAn able-bodied person performs necessary bodily work rather than expecting others to do every task
SwadeshiDuty towards nearby people and reasonable preference for locally produced goodsA person chooses locally available necessities that adequately meet the need
Sarvatra-bhaya-varjana or FearlessnessFreedom from fear that prevents a person from following truth and dutyA person calmly reports wrongdoing despite fear of disapproval
Sparshabhavana or Removal of UntouchabilityRejection of untouchability and recognition of equal human dignityPeople refuse to exclude a classmate or neighbour because of caste
Sarva-dharma-samabhava or Equal Respect for ReligionsRespect for people of different religious faithsA person treats neighbours of other faiths with the same respect given to members of their own faith

Bread Labour: Respect for bodily work

Sharir-shrama means physical labour, also called Bread Labour. Gandhi believed that useful bodily work should form part of the life of an able-bodied individual. The principle opposes the assumption that manual labour is inferior or should always be performed by someone else.

Bread Labour does not mean that intellectual work has no value. It means that intellectual activity should not become an excuse for avoiding all bodily effort. Gandhi's account also recognised the responsibility to care for children, older people, people with disabilities and those who are ill.

Swadeshi as an ashram vow

Swadeshi appears both as a wider Gandhian concept and as one of the 11 vows. As an observance, it asks the individual to recognise duties towards the immediate community. Giving reasonable priority to nearby people and locally available goods is an expression of that responsibility.

It must not be confused with hostility towards distant communities. For Gandhi, service to those nearby was consistent with concern for humanity as a whole.

Fearlessness is not aggression

Sarvatra-bhaya-varjana refers to freedom from fear. Gandhi considered fearlessness important because fear may lead a person to conceal the truth, remain silent about wrongdoing or abandon a moral duty.

Fearlessness should not be interpreted as a licence to threaten others. A person who calmly speaks the truth despite social pressure demonstrates fearlessness. A person who intimidates others demonstrates aggression, which conflicts with ahimsa.

Removal of untouchability and equal dignity

Sparshabhavana is associated with the rejection and removal of untouchability. It calls for the recognition of the equal human dignity of people who have been subjected to caste-based exclusion.

The principle is not fulfilled merely by expressing sympathy while continuing to treat some people as inferior or impure. Its essential meaning is the rejection of exclusion based on untouchability.

This vow connects directly with ahimsa because social humiliation and discrimination are inconsistent with the obligation to respect other people.

Equal respect for religions

The final vow is described as tolerance in the Rajghat account and is also associated with Sarva-dharma-samabhava, meaning equal regard or respect for religions. Related transliterations include Sarva Dharma Samantva.

The idea requires respect for the religious beliefs of others, not merely a grudging willingness to let them exist. It does not require every person to adopt the same religious beliefs or to claim that all religious doctrines are identical.

A person may remain committed to a particular faith while showing genuine respect towards followers of other faiths. This is the distinction between equal respect and uniform belief.

Recognising all 11 vows together

The complete set consists of Satya, Ahimsa, Brahmacharya, Asvada, Asteya, Aparigraha, Sharir-shrama, Swadeshi, Sarvatra-bhaya-varjana, Sparshabhavana and Sarva-dharma-samabhava. The first 6 were explained through truthfulness, non-injury, personal restraint and possessions. The remaining 5 concern useful labour, local responsibility, courage, equality and respect for religions.

They can also be connected with the wider ideas of Gandhi's thought. Satya and ahimsa guide the choice of moral means. Sarvodaya is the welfare of all, while trusteeship asks holders of wealth to recognise social responsibility. Swadeshi emphasises local duty, and gram swaraj develops the idea of participatory village self-rule. Hind Swaraj (1909) explains self-rule as more than a change of rulers. Nai Talim, associated with the Wardha Scheme of 1937, integrates education with productive work.

Common distinctions for concept identification

  • Truthfulness versus courage: speaking accurately concerns satya; overcoming fear in order to speak concerns fearlessness. Both may be present in the same action.
  • Non-stealing versus non-possession: asteya concerns what a person may rightfully take or use; aparigraha concerns unnecessary accumulation.
  • Bread Labour versus Nai Talim: Bread Labour is an ethical duty to undertake useful physical work; Nai Talim makes productive work central to education.
  • Swadeshi versus gram swaraj: swadeshi emphasises local responsibility; gram swaraj is the broader ideal of village self-rule.
  • Equal religious respect versus identical belief: respect for different faiths does not require everyone to hold the same beliefs.
  • Trusteeship versus aparigraha: trusteeship focuses on the social responsibility of a resource-holder; aparigraha is the personal discipline of avoiding unnecessary possessions.

Prelims focus

  • Sharir-shrama: Bread Labour or useful bodily work.
  • Swadeshi: duty towards one's immediate surroundings and preference for local goods.
  • Sarvatra-bhaya-varjana: fearlessness.
  • Sparshabhavana: removal of untouchability.
  • Sarva-dharma-samabhava: equal respect for religions.
  • Trap: Fearlessness does not mean aggression; religious respect does not mean that all beliefs must be identical.

[Sources: Rajghat Samadhi Committee, Government of India, The Eleven Vows of Gandhi Ji, observances VII–XI, consulted 22 November 2026; Mani Bhavan Gandhi Sangrahalaya, Gandhi's Eleven Vows, sections on Bread Labour, Swadeshi, Fearlessness, Removal of Untouchability and Equality of Religions, consulted 22 November 2026; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 11, chapter 3, printed pp. 31–38; Ministry of Culture, Government of India, Gandhi Heritage Portal: The Key Texts, release dated 1 October 2013; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, Dr Zakir Husain Memorial Lecture, release dated 2 March 2009, Wardha Scheme resolutions.]
